title: Three o'clock
hookLine: the hour of Christ's death, kept as an hour of mercy

lines: PETER AND JOHN GO UP TO PRAY.
cards: In Acts, Peter and John are walking up to the Temple in the middle of the afternoon. Not to preach, but to pray, at an hour set aside for it. At the gate, a man who has never walked asks them for money.
The same hour turns up in the Gospels, on an afternoon when, Mark says, darkness covered the land. And some Catholics still mark it, by the clock, every day.

teach.b: The Gospels count the day's hours from morning, so their ninth hour falls in the middle of the afternoon, and Catholic tradition keeps it at three.
Acts says it plainly, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now Peter and John went up into the temple at the ninth hour of prayer." An hour of prayer, already, before it meant anything more.

Mark tells of darkness over the land from the sixth hour until the ninth, and places Jesus's death at the ninth. Luke gives his last words: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." Then he breathes his last.
For Christians, the afternoon hour of prayer became the hour he died.

The Church's own prayer kept the hour. The Liturgy of the Hours has a short mid-afternoon office called None, the ninth. Monks and sisters stop their work for it; so do some lay people with a prayer book in a desk drawer.
In her diary, Faustina wrote that Jesus asked her to honor the hour of his death, at three o'clock, and to ask then for mercy, especially for sinners.
She records that even a brief moment was enough: a thought of the cross while carrying on with her work. So in some Catholic hospitals and parishes, a bell or a voice marks three.

teach.h: FATHER, INTO THY HANDS I COMMEND MY SPIRIT.
teach.b: Some people pray the chaplet then. Some pause for a few seconds at a desk, in traffic, in a checkout line. None of it is required.
That's the shape of a devotion: an ordinary minute of an ordinary afternoon, turned toward one afternoon on a hill outside Jerusalem.

how: Some Catholics pause at three in the afternoon, the hour tradition gives for Jesus's death, to pray the Divine Mercy chaplet or simply to remember the cross; religious communities pray the mid-afternoon hour of the Liturgy of the Hours.

o: the hour Jesus rose from the dead on Easter
the ninth hour, an old hour of prayer and mercy
the time of the Church's only daily Mass

p: went up to pray at the ninth hour
an hour to ask for mercy

s: the Gospels say Jesus died at exactly 3:00 p.m.
they speak of the ninth hour, counted from morning. tradition keeps it at three.
in Acts, the ninth hour was already an hour of prayer
Peter and John went up into the Temple at the ninth hour of prayer.
Catholics are required to stop and pray at three
it's a devotion, freely chosen. Faustina wrote that even a brief moment was enough.

games.q: you're Peter, on your way up to the Temple at the hour of prayer. at the gate, a man who has never walked asks you for money. you have none. what do you do?
o: walk past, or you'll be late for prayer.
tell him you have no silver or gold, and give what you do have.
promise to come back after prayer.
games.why: Peter says he has no silver or gold, but gives what he has: in the name of Jesus, he tells the man to get up and walk, and he does. on the way to prayer, the prayer happened at the gate.

practice: Think of where you'll be at three this afternoon, a desk, a kitchen, a car, and choose one tiny sign for that moment: setting down whatever's in your hands, one slow breath, the sign of the cross.
If you pray, borrow Jesus's words from Luke, Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit, or ask mercy for someone who's suffering; if you don't, let three o'clock be a moment to remember that person.

wordCard.voice: Three o'clock. The ninth hour: an old hour of prayer, the hour the Gospels give for Jesus's death, and in Faustina's devotion, the hour of mercy.

carryVoice: Your line: the hour of mercy. Even a brief moment, Faustina wrote, was enough. See you tomorrow.
